eu_legal.definition: A food additive is any substance not normally consumed as a food in itself and not normally used as a characteristic ingredient of food, whether or not it has nutritive value, the intentional addition of which to food for a technological purpose in the manufacture, processing, preparation, treatment, packaging, transport or storage of such food results, or may be reasonably expected to result, in it or its by-products becoming directly or indirectly a component of such foods
not_additives: monosaccharides, disaccharides or oligosaccharides and foods containing these substances used for their sweetening properties

foods, whether dried or in concentrated form, including flavourings incorporated during the manufacturing of compound foods, because of their aromatic, sapid or nutritive properties together with a secondary colouring effect
substances used in covering or coating materials, which do not form part of foods and are not intended to be consumed together with those foods

products containing pectin and derived from dried apple pomace or peel of citrus fruits or quinces, or from a mixture of them, by the action of dilute acid followed by partial neutralisation with sodium or potassium salts (liquid pectin)
white or yellow dextrin, roasted or dextrinated starch, starch modified by acid or alkali treatment, bleached starch, physically modified starch and starch treated by amylolitic enzymes
blood plasma, edible gelatin, protein hydrolysates and their salts, milk protein and gluten
amino acids and their salts other than glutamic acid, glycine, cysteine and cystine and their salts having no technological function
eu_legal.processing_aid: A processing aid is any substance which: is not consumed as a food by itself; is intentionally used in the processing of raw materials, foods or their ingredients, to fulfil a certain technological purpose during treatment or processing; and may result in the unintentional but technically unavoidable presence in the final product of residues of the substance or its derivatives provided they do not present any health risk and do not have any technological effect on the final product

conditions.intro: A food additive may be included in the Community lists in Annexes II and III only if it meets the following conditions and, where relevant, other legitimate factors, including environmental factors
items: it does not, on the basis of the scientific evidence available, pose a safety concern to the health of the consumer at the level of use proposed
there is a reasonable technological need that cannot be achieved by other economically and technologically practicable means
its use does not mislead the consumer

purposes.intro: To be included in the Community lists in Annexes II and III a food additive must have advantages and benefits for the consumer and therefore serve one or more of the following purposes
items: preserving the nutritional quality of the food
providing necessary ingredients or constituents for foods manufactured for groups of consumers with special dietary needs

enhancing the keeping quality or stability of a food or improving its organoleptic properties, provided that the nature, substance or quality of the food is not changed in such a way as to mislead the consumer

aiding in the manufacture, processing, preparation, treatment, packing, transport or storage of food, including food additives, food enzymes and food flavourings, provided that the food additive is not used to disguise the effects of the use of faulty raw materials or of any undesirable practices or techniques, including unhygienic practices or techniques, during the course of any such activities

functional_classes.name: sweeteners
functional_classes.definition: Substances used to impart a sweet taste to foods or in table-top sweeteners

functional_classes.name: colours
functional_classes.definition: Substances which add or restore colour in a food, and include natural constituents of foods and natural sources which are normally not consumed as foods as such and not normally used as characteristic ingredients of food. Preparations obtained from foods and other edible natural source materials obtained by physical and/or chemical extraction resulting in a selective extraction of the pigments relative to the nutritive or aromatic constituents are colours within the meaning of this Regulation

functional_classes.name: preservatives
functional_classes.definition: Substances which prolong the shelf-life of foods by protecting them against deterioration caused by micro-organisms and/or which protect against growth of pathogenic micro-organisms

functional_classes.name: antioxidants
functional_classes.definition: Substances which prolong the shelf-life of foods by protecting them against deterioration caused by oxidation, such as fat rancidity and colour changes

functional_classes.name: carriers
functional_classes.definition: Substances used to dissolve, dilute, disperse or otherwise physically modify a food additive or a flavouring, food enzyme, nutrient and/or other substance added for nutritional or physiological purposes to a food without altering its function (and without exerting any technological effect themselves) in order to facilitate its handling, application or use

functional_classes.name: acids
functional_classes.definition: Substances which increase the acidity of a foodstuff and/or impart a sour taste to it

functional_classes.name: acidity regulators
functional_classes.definition: Substances which alter or control the acidity or alkalinity of a foodstuff

functional_classes.name: anti-caking agents
functional_classes.definition: Substances which reduce the tendency of individual particles of a foodstuff to adhere to one another

functional_classes.name: anti-foaming agents
functional_classes.definition: Substances which prevent or reduce foaming

functional_classes.name: bulking agents
functional_classes.definition: Substances which contribute to the volume of a foodstuff without contributing significantly to its available energy value

functional_classes.name: emulsifiers
functional_classes.definition: Substances which make it possible to form or maintain a homogenous mixture of two or more immiscible phases such as oil and water in a foodstuff

functional_classes.name: emulsifying salts
functional_classes.definition: Substances which convert proteins contained in cheese into a dispersed form and thereby bring about homogenous distribution of fat and other components

functional_classes.name: firming agents
functional_classes.definition: Substances which make or keep tissues of fruit or vegetables firm or crisp, or interact with gelling agents to produce or strengthen a gel

functional_classes.name: flavour enhancers
functional_classes.definition: Substances which enhance the existing taste and/or odour of a foodstuff

functional_classes.name: foaming agents
functional_classes.definition: Substances which make it possible to form a homogenous dispersion of a gaseous phase in a liquid or solid foodstuff

functional_classes.name: gelling agents
functional_classes.definition: Substances which give a foodstuff texture through formation of a gel

functional_classes.name: glazing agents
functional_classes.definition: Substances which, when applied to the external surface of a foodstuff, impart a shiny appearance or provide a protective coating

functional_classes.name: humectants
functional_classes.definition: Substances which prevent foods from drying out by counteracting the effect of an atmosphere having a low degree of humidity, or promote the dissolution of a powder in an aqueous medium

functional_classes.name: modified starches
functional_classes.definition: Substances obtained by one or more chemical treatments of edible starches, which may have undergone a physical or enzymatic treatment, and may be acid or alkali thinned or bleached

functional_classes.name: packaging gases
functional_classes.definition: Gases other than air, introduced into a container before, during or after the placing of a foodstuff in that container

functional_classes.name: propellants
functional_classes.definition: Gases other than air which expel a foodstuff from a container

functional_classes.name: raising agents
functional_classes.definition: Substances or combinations of substances which liberate gas and thereby increase the volume of a dough or a batter

functional_classes.name: sequestrants
functional_classes.definition: Substances which form chemical complexes with metallic ions

functional_classes.name: stabilisers
functional_classes.definition: Substances which make it possible to maintain the physico-chemical state of a foodstuff; stabilisers include substances which enable the maintenance of a homogenous dispersion of two or more immiscible substances in a foodstuff, substances which stabilise, retain or intensify colour of a foodstuff and substances which increase the binding capacity of the food, including the formation of cross-links between proteins enabling the binding of food pieces into re-constituted food

functional_classes.name: thickeners
functional_classes.definition: Substances which increase the viscosity of a foodstuff

functional_classes.name: flour treatment agents
functional_classes.definition: Substances, other than emulsifiers, which are added to flour or dough to improve its baking quality

functional_classes.name: contrast enhancers
functional_classes.definition: Substances which, when applied to the external surface of fruit or vegetables following depigmentation of predefined parts (e.g. by laser treatment), help to distinguish these parts from the remaining surface by imparting colour following interaction with certain components of the epidermis

identity.definition: Curcumin is obtained by solvent extraction of turmeric i.e. the ground rhizomes of strains of Curcuma longa L. In order to obtain a concentrated curcumin powder, the extract is purified by crystallization. The product consists essentially of curcumins; i.e. the colouring principle (1,7-bis(4-hydroxy-3-methoxyphenyl)hepta-1,6-dien-3,5-dione) and its two desmethoxy derivatives in varying proportions. Minor amounts of oils and resins naturally occurring in turmeric may be present. Curcumin is also used as the aluminium lake; the aluminium content is less than 30 %. Only the following solvents may be used in the extraction: ethylacetate, acetone, carbon dioxide, dichloromethane, n-butanol, methanol, ethanol, hexane, propan-2-ol.

identity.definition: Tartrazine is prepared from 4-amino-benzenesulphonic acid, which is diazotized using hydrochloric acid and sodium nitrite. The diazo compound is then coupled with 4,5-dihydro-5-oxo-1-(4sulphophenyl)-1H-pyrazole-3-carboxylic acid or with the methyl ester, the ethyl ester, or a salt of this carboxylic acid. The resulting dye is purified and isolated as the sodium salt. Tartrazine consists essentially of trisodium 5-hydroxy-1-(4-sulfonatophenyl)-4-(4-sulfonatophenylazo)-H-pyrazole-3-carboxylate and subsidiary colouring matters together with sodium chloride and/or sodium sulphate as the principal uncoloured components. Tartrazine is described as the sodium salt. The calcium and the potassium salt are also permitted.

overview: Tartrazine (E 102) is a food additive. The official lists name this function: colour.
The EU specification describes it as: “Light orange powder or granules.”
In the EU it may be used in 37 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; edible ices; fruit and vegetables; confectionery…
In the US it is listed as FD&C Yellow No. 5: certified colour additive for food (21 CFR 74.705).
Canada permits it (on the List of Permitted Food Colours).
Australia and New Zealand permit it as a food additive.

identity.definition: Sunset Yellow FCF consists essentially of disodium 2-hydroxy-1-(4-sulfonatophenylazo) naphthalene-6-sulfonate and subsidiary colouring matters together with sodium chloride and/or sodium sulphate as the principal uncoloured components. Sunset Yellow FCF is manufactured by diazotizing 4-aminobenzenesulphonic acid using hydrochloric acid and sodium nitrite or sulphuric acid and sodium nitrite. The diazo compound is coupled with 6-hydroxy-2-naphthalene-sulphonic acid. The dye is isolated as the sodium salt and dried. Sunset Yellow FCF is described as the sodium salt. The calcium and the potassium salt are also permitted.

overview: Sunset Yellow FCF/Orange Yellow S (E 110) is a food additive. The official lists name this function: colour.
The EU specification describes it as: “Orange-red powder or granules.”
In the EU it may be used in 27 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; fruit and vegetables; confectionery; cereals and cereal products…
In the US it is listed as FD&C Yellow No. 6: certified colour additive for food (21 CFR 74.706).
Canada permits it as Sunset Yellow FCF (on the List of Permitted Food Colours).
Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Sunset yellow FCF) as a food additive.

identity.definition: Carminic acid is obtained from aqueous, aqueous alcoholic or alcoholic extracts from Cochineal, which consists of the dried bodies of the female insect Dactylopius coccus Costa. Carmines are aluminium lakes of carminic acid in which aluminium and carminic acid are thought to be present in the molar ratio 1:2. The colouring principle is carminic acid. Minor amounts of its aminated form 4-aminocarminic acid may also be present. In commercial products the colouring principle carminic acid may be present in association with ammonium, calcium, potassium or sodium cations, singly or in combination, and these cations may also be present in excess. Commercial products may also contain proteinaceous material derived from the source insect.
identity.description: Red to dark red, friable, solid or powder
identity.assay: Content not less than 90 % carminic acid; not less than 50 % carminic acid in the chelates.
identification: Carminic acid: Maximum in aqueous ammonia solution at ca. 518 nm Maximum in dilute hydrochloric solution at ca. 494 nm E 1 %/1 cm 139 at peak around 494 nm in dilute hydrochloric acid 4-aminocarminic acid: Maximum in aqueous ammonia solution at 535 nm Maximum in dilute hydrochloric solution at 530 n

overview: Carminic acid, Carmine (E 120) is a food additive. The official lists name this function: colour.
The EU specification describes it as: “Red to dark red, friable, solid or powder.”
In the EU it may be used in 46 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; edible ices; fruit and vegetables; confectionery…
In the US it is listed as Carmine (Coccus Cacti L.): colour additive for food, exempt from certification (21 CFR 73.100).
Canada permits it as Cochineal (on the List of Permitted Food Colours).
Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Cochineal or carmines or carminic acid) as a food additive.

overview: Allura Red AC (E 129) is a food additive. The official lists name this function: colour.
The EU specification describes it as: “Dark red powder or granules.”
In the EU it may be used in 41 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; edible ices; fruit and vegetables; confectionery…
In the US it is listed as FD&C Red No. 40: certified colour additive for food (21 CFR 74.340).
Canada permits it as Allura Red (on the List of Permitted Food Colours).
Australia and New Zealand permit it as a food additive.

identity.definition: Indigotine consists essentially of a mixture of disodium 3,3′dioxo-2,2′-bi-indolylidene-5,5′-disulfonate, and disodium 3,3′-dioxo-2,2′-bi-indolylidene-5,7′-disulfonate and subsidiary colouring matters together with sodium chloride and/or sodium sulphate as the principal uncoloured components. Indigotine is described as the sodium salt. The calcium and the potassium salt are also permitted. Indigo carmine is obtained by sulphonation of indigo. This is accomplished by heating indigo (or indigo paste) in the presence of sulphuric acid. The dye is isolated and subjected to purification procedures.

identity.definition: Chlorophylls are obtained by solvent extraction of strains of edible plant material, grass, lucerne and nettle. During the subsequent removal of solvent, the naturally present coordinated magnesium may be wholly or partly removed from the chlorophylls to give the corresponding phaeophytins. The principal colouring matters are the phaeophytins and magnesium chlorophylls. The extracted product, from which the solvent has been removed, contains other pigments such as carotenoids as well as oils, fats and waxes derived from the source material. Only the following solvents may be used for the extraction: acetone, methyl ethyl ketone, dichloromethane, carbon dioxide, methanol, ethanol, propan-2-ol and hexane.

identity.definition: Copper chlorophylls are obtained by addition of a salt of copper to the substance obtained by solvent extraction of strains of edible plant material, grass, lucerne, and nettle. The product, from which the solvent has been removed, contains other pigments such as carotenoids as well as fats and waxes derived from the source material. The principal colouring matters are the copper phaeophytins. Only the following solvents may be used for the extraction: acetone, methyl ethyl ketone, dichloromethane, carbon dioxide, methanol, ethanol, propan-2-ol and hexane.
identity.description: Waxy solid ranging in colour from blue green to dark green depending on the source material
identity.mw: Copper chlorophyll a: 932,75 Copper chlorophyll b: 946,73
identity.assay: Content of total copper chlorophylls is not less than 10 %. 540 at ca. 422 nm in chloroform 300 at ca. 652 nm in chloroform
identification: Maximum in chloroform at ca. 422 nm and at ca. 652 nm

overview: Copper complexes of chlorophylls, chlorophyllins (E 141) is a food additive. The official lists name this function: colour.
The EU specification describes it as: “Waxy solid ranging in colour from blue green to dark green depending on the source material.”
In the EU it may be used in 48 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; edible ices; fruit and vegetables; confectionery…
In the US it is listed as Sodium Copper Chlorophyllin: colour additive for food, exempt from certification (21 CFR 73.125).
Canada permits it as Sodium Copper Chlorophyllin; Sodium Potassium Copper Chlorophyllin (on 2 of Health Canada's permitted lists).
Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Chlorophyll-copper complex; Chlorophyllin copper complex, sodium and potassium salts) as a food additive.

overview: Plain caramel (E 150a) is a food additive. The official lists name this function: colour.
The EU specification describes it as: “Dark brown to black liquids or solids.”
In the EU it may be used in 55 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; edible ices; fruit and vegetables; confectionery…
In the US it is listed as Caramel: colour additive for food, exempt from certification (21 CFR 73.85).
Canada permits it as Caramel (on the List of Permitted Food Colours).
Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Caramel I) as a food additive.

overview: Ammonia caramel (E 150c) is a food additive. The official lists name this function: colour.
The EU specification describes it as: “Dark brown to black liquids or solids.”
In the EU it may be used in 44 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; edible ices; fruit and vegetables; confectionery…
In the US it is listed as Caramel: colour additive for food, exempt from certification (21 CFR 73.85).
Canada permits it as Caramel (on the List of Permitted Food Colours).
Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Caramel III) as a food additive.

identity.definition: Vegetable activated carbon is produced by the carbonisation of vegetable material such as wood, cellulose residues, peat and coconut and other shells. The activated carbon thus produced is milled by a roller mill and the resulting highly activated powdered carbon is treated by a cyclone. The fine fractio40800n from the cyclone is purified by hydrochloric acid washing, neutralised and then dried. The resulting product is what is known traditionally as vegetable black. Products with a higher colouring power are produced from the fine fraction by a further cyclone treatment or by extra milling, followed by acid washing, neutralising and drying. It consists essentially of finely divided carbon. It may contain minor amounts of nitrogen, hydrogen and oxygen. Some moisture may be absorbed on the product after manufacture.
identity.description: Black, odourless powder
identity.assay: Content not less than 95 % of carbon calculated on an anhydrous and ash-free basis
identity.solubility: Insoluble in water and organic solvents
identification: Insoluble in water and organic solvents
When heated to redness it burns slowly without a flame
purity: Benzo(a)pyrene less than 50 μg/kg in the extract obtained by extraction of 1 g of the product with 10 g pure cyclohexane in a continuous extraction.

identity.definition: Solvent-extracted bixin is obtained by the extraction of the outer coating of the seeds of the annatto tree (Bixa orellana L.) with one or more of the following food grade solvents: acetone, methanol, hexane, ethanol, isopropyl alcohol, ethyl acetate, alkaline alcohol or supercritical carbon dioxide. The resulting preparation may be acidified, followed by the removal of the solvent, drying and milling. Solvent-extracted bixin contains several coloured components; the major colouring principle is cis-bixin, a minor colouring principle is trans-bixin; thermal degradation products of bixin may also be present as a result of processing.

identity.definition: Solvent-extracted norbixin is obtained from the outer coating of the seeds of the annatto tree (Bixa orellana L.) by washing with one or more of the following food grade solvents: acetone, methanol, hexane, ethanol, isopropyl alcohol, ethyl acetate, alkaline alcohol or supercritical carbon dioxide followed by solvent removal, crystallization and drying. Aqueous alkali is added to the resultant powder, which is then heated to hydrolyse the colouring matter and cooled. The aqueous solution is filtered, and acidified to precipitate the norbixin. The precipitate is filtered, washed, dried and milled, to give a granular powder. Solvent-extracted norbixin contains several coloured components; the major colouring principle is cis-norbixin, a minor colouring principle is trans-norbixin; thermal degradation products of norbixin may also be present as a result of processing.

identity.definition: Synthetic lycopene is a mixture of geometric isomeres of lycopenes and is produced by the Wittig condensation of synthetic intermediates commonly used in the production of other carotenoids used in food. Synthetic lycopene consists predominantly of all-trans-lycopene together with 5-cis-lycopene and minor quantities of other isomers. Commercial lycopene preparations intended for use in food are formulated as suspensions in edible oils or water-dispersible or water-soluble powder.

identity.definition: Beet red is obtained from the roots of strains of red beets (Beta vulgaris L. var. rubra) by pressing crushed beet as press juice or by aqueous extraction of shredded beet roots and subsequent enrichment in the active principle. The colour is composed of different pigments all belonging to the class betalaine. The main colouring principle consists of betacyanins (red) of which betanin accounts for 75-95 %. Minor amounts of betaxanthin (yellow) and degradation products of betalaines (light brown) may be present. Besides the colour pigments the juice or extract consists of sugars, salts, and/or proteins naturally occurring in red beets. The solution may be concentrated and some products may be refined in order to remove most of the sugars, salts and proteins.
identity.description: Red or dark red liquid, paste, powder or solid

identification: Maximum in water of pH 5 at ca. 535 nm
purity: Not more than 2 g nitrate anion/g of red colour (as calculated from assay).

identity.definition: Anthocyanins are obtained by maceration or extraction with sulphited water, acidified water, carbon dioxide, methanol or ethanol from the strains of vegetables and edible fruits, with subsequent concentration and/or purification if necessary. The resulting product can be transformed into powder by an industrial drying process. Anthocyanins contain common components of the source material, namely anthocyanine, organic acids, tannins, sugars, minerals etc., but not necessarily in the same proportions as found in the source material. Ethanol may naturally be present as a result of the maceration process. The colouring principle is anthocyanin. Products are marketed according to their colour strength as determined by the assay. Colour content is not expressed using quantitative units.

identity.definition: Titanium dioxide consists essentially of pure anatase and/or rutile titanium dioxide which may be coated with small amounts of alumina and/or silica to improve the technological properties of the product. The anatase grades of pigmentary titanium dioxide can only be made by the sulphate process which creates a large amount of sulphuric acid as a by-product. The rutile grades of titanium dioxide are typically made by the chloride process. Certain rutile grades of titanium dioxide are produced using mica (also known as potassium aluminum silicate) as a template to form the basic platelet structure. The surface of the mica is coated with titanium dioxide using a specialised patented process. Rutile titanium dioxide, platelet form is manufactured by subjecting titanium dioxide (rutile) coated mica nacreous pigment to an extractive dissolution in acid followed by an extractive dissolution in alkali. All of the mica is removed during this process and the resulting product is a platelet form of rutile titanium dioxide.

overview: Sorbic acid (E 200) is a food additive. The official lists name this function: preservative.

The EU specification describes it as: “Colourless needles or white free flowing crystalline powder, having a slight characteristic odour and showing no change in colour after heating for 90 minutes at 105 °C.”
In the EU it may be used in 59 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; fats and oils and fat and oil emulsions; fruit and vegetables; confectionery…
In the US it is listed as Sorbic Acid: listed as GRAS (21 CFR 182).
Canada permits it (on the List of Permitted Preservatives).
Australia and New Zealand permit it in specific foods (Schedule 15 of the Food Standards Code).

overview: Sodium benzoate (E 211) is a food additive. The official lists name this function: preservative.
The EU specification describes it as: “A white, almost odourless, crystalline powder or granules.”
In the EU it may be used in 32 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; fruit and vegetables; confectionery; meat…
In the US it is listed as Sodium Benzoate: affirmed as GRAS (21 CFR 184).
Canada permits it (on the List of Permitted Preservatives).
Australia and New Zealand permit it in specific foods (Schedule 15 of the Food Standards Code).

identity.description: White crystalline powder
identity.assay: Content not less than 99 % C7H5KO2 after drying at 105 °C to constant weight
identification: Melting range of benzoic acid isolated by acidification and not recrystallised 121,5 °C to 123,5 °C, after vacuum drying in a sulphuric acid desiccator
purity: Not more than 0,06 % expressed as chloride, corresponding to 0,25 % expressed as monochlorobenzoic acid

Add 1,5 ml of sulphuric acid to 100 ml of water, heat to boiling point and add 0,1 N KMnO4 in drops, until the pink colour persists for 30 seconds. Dissolve 1 g of the sample, weighed to the nearest mg, in the heated solution, and titrate with 0,1 N KMnO4 to a pink colour that persists for 15 second

A cold solution of 0,5 g of benzoic acid in 5 ml 94,5 to 95,5 % sulphuric acid must not show a stronger colouring than that of a reference liquid containing 0,2 ml of cobalt chloride TSC, 0,3 ml of ferric chloride TSC, 0,1 ml of copper sulphate TSC and 4,4 ml of water
On fractional acidification of a (neutralised) solution of potassium benzoate, the first precipitate must not have a different melting range from that of benzoic acid
Neutralisation of 1 g of potassium benzoate, in the presence of phenolphthalein, must not require more than 0,25 ml of 0,1 N NaOH or 0,1 N HCl

overview: Methyl p-hydroxybenzoate (E 218) is a food additive. The official lists name this function: preservative.
The EU specification describes it as: “Almost odourless, small colourless crystals or white crystalline powder.”
In the EU it may be used in 8 food categories, in these food groups: confectionery; meat; sugars, syrups, honey and table-top sweeteners; ready-to-eat savouries and snacks.
In the US it is listed as Methyl P-Hydroxybenzoate: affirmed as GRAS (21 CFR 184).
Canada permits it as Methyl-ρ-Hydroxybenzoate (on the List of Permitted Preservatives).
Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Methylparaben or Methyl-p-hydroxy- benzoate) in specific foods (Schedule 15 of the Food Standards Code).

overview: Sulphur dioxide (E 220) is a food additive. The official lists name these functions: acidity regulator and preservative.
The EU specification describes it as: “Colourless, non-flammable gas with strong pungent suffocating odour.”
In the EU it may be used in 40 food categories, in these food groups: fruit and vegetables; confectionery; cereals and cereal products; bakery wares…
In the US it is listed as Sulfur Dioxide: colour additive for food, exempt from certification (21 CFR 73.170).
Canada permits it as Sulphurous Acid (on 2 of Health Canada's permitted lists).
Australia and New Zealand permit it in specific foods (Schedule 15 of the Food Standards Code).

overview: Sodium sulphite (E 221) is a food additive. The official lists name these functions: flour treatment agent, colour and preservative.
The EU specification describes it as: “White crystalline powder or colourless crystals.”
In the EU it may be used in 40 food categories, in these food groups: fruit and vegetables; confectionery; cereals and cereal products; bakery wares…
In the US it is listed as Sodium Sulfite: listed as GRAS (21 CFR 182).
Canada permits it (on 3 of Health Canada's permitted lists).
Australia and New Zealand permit it in specific foods (Schedule 15 of the Food Standards Code).

overview: Sodium hydrogen sulphite (E 222) is a food additive. The official lists name this function: preservative.
The EU specification describes it as: “A clear, colourless to yellow solution.”
In the EU it may be used in 40 food categories, in these food groups: fruit and vegetables; confectionery; cereals and cereal products; bakery wares…
In the US it is listed as Sodium Bisulfite: listed as GRAS (21 CFR 182).
Canada permits it as Sodium Bisulphite (on the List of Permitted Preservatives).
Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Sodium bisulphite) in specific foods (Schedule 15 of the Food Standards Code).

rows.max: (a) If used singly, the amount not to exceed 500 ppm, calculated as sulphur dioxide. If used in any combination with potassium bisulphite, potassium metabisulphite, sodium bisulphite, sodium dithionite, sodium sulphite or sulphurous acid, the total combined amount not to exceed 500 ppm, calculated as sulphur dioxide.

(b) If used singly, the amount not to exceed 15 ppm, calculated as sulphur dioxide. If used in any combination with potassium bisulphite, potassium metabisulphite, sodium bisulphite, sodium dithionite, sodium sulphite or sulphurous acid, the total combined amount not to exceed 15 ppm, calculated as sulphur dioxide.
(c) Good Manufacturing Practice. The amount not to exceed 100 ppm in the edible portion of the uncooked food, calculated as sulphur dioxide.

rows.foods: (d) Cider; Fruit wine; Honey wine; Wine
rows.max: (d) Good Manufacturing Practice. The amount of sodium metabisulphite, added singly or in any combination with potassium bisulphite, potassium metabisulphite, sodium bisulphite, sodium dithionite, sodium sulphite or sulphurous acid, not to exceed 70 ppm in the free state in the finished product, calculated as sulphur dioxide, or 350 ppm in the combined state in the finished product, calculated as sulphur dioxide.

(e) Good Manufacturing Practice. May be used singly or in any combination with potassium bisulphite, potassium metabisulphite, sodium bisulphite, sodium dithionite, sodium sulphite or sulphurous acid. In either case, the total amount not to exceed 100 ppm in the edible portion of the uncooked food, calculated as sulphur dioxide.

(f) If used singly, the amount not to exceed 20 ppm, calculated as sulphur dioxide. If used in any combination with potassium bisulphite, potassium metabisulphite, sodium bisulphite, sodium dithionite, sodium sulphite or sulphurous acid, the total combined amount not to exceed 20 ppm, calculated as sulphur dioxide.

(g) If used singly, the amount not to exceed 2,500 ppm, calculated as sulphur dioxide. If used in any combination with potassium bisulphite, potassium metabisulphite, sodium bisulphite, sodium dithionite, sodium sulphite or sulphurous acid, the total combined amount not to exceed 2,500 ppm, calculated as sulphur dioxide.

overview: Sodium metabisulphite (E 223) is a food additive. The official lists name this function: preservative.
The EU specification describes it as: “White crystals or crystalline powder.”
In the EU it may be used in 40 food categories, in these food groups: fruit and vegetables; confectionery; cereals and cereal products; bakery wares…
In the US it is listed as Sodium Metabisulfite: listed as GRAS (21 CFR 182).
Canada permits it (on the List of Permitted Preservatives).
Australia and New Zealand permit it in specific foods (Schedule 15 of the Food Standards Code).

overview: Potassium metabisulphite (E 224) is a food additive. The official lists name this function: preservative.
The EU specification describes it as: “Colourless crystals or white crystalline powder.”
In the EU it may be used in 40 food categories, in these food groups: fruit and vegetables; confectionery; cereals and cereal products; bakery wares…
In the US it is listed as Potassium Metabisulfite: listed as GRAS (21 CFR 182).
Canada permits it (on the List of Permitted Preservatives).
Australia and New Zealand permit it in specific foods (Schedule 15 of the Food Standards Code).

overview: Calcium hydrogen sulphite (E 227) is a food additive.
The EU specification describes it as: “Clear greenish-yellow aqueous solution having a distinct odour of sulphur dioxide.”
In the EU it may be used in 40 food categories, in these food groups: fruit and vegetables; confectionery; cereals and cereal products; bakery wares…

ca_uses.title: List of Permitted Preservatives

rows.foods: (a) Cover pickle or dry cure used in the curing of preserved meat or preserved meat by-product prepared by slow cure processes
rows.max: (a) Good manufacturing practice. If used singly or in combination with potassium nitrate, the total amount of such nitrate salts added to each batch of preserved meat or preserved meat by-product not to exceed 200 ppm, calculated prior to any smoking, cooking or fermentation. When sodium nitrate is included in the cover pickle or dry cure that is sold for use in preserved meat or preserved meat by-product, it must be packaged separately from any spice or seasoning.

rows.foods: (b) Dry sausage, semi-dry sausage, preserved meat or preserved meat by-product prepared by slow cure processes
rows.max: (b) If used singly, the amount added to each batch of dry sausage, semi-dry sausage, preserved meat or preserved meat by-product not to exceed 200 ppm, calculated prior to any smoking, cooking or fermentation. If used in combination with potassium nitrate, the total combined amount added to each batch of dry sausage, semi-dry sausage, preserved meat or preserved meat by-product not to exceed 200 ppm, calculated prior to any smoking, cooking or fermentation.

rows.foods: (c) Meat binder for dry sausage, semi-dry sausage, preserved meat or preserved meat by-product prepared by slow cure processes
rows.max: (c) Good manufacturing practice. If used singly or in combination with potassium nitrate, the total amount of such nitrate salts added to each batch of dry sausage, semi-dry sausage, preserved meat or preserved meat by-product not to exceed 200 ppm, calculated prior to any smoking, cooking or fermentation. When sodium nitrate is included in the meat binder that is sold for use in dry sausage, semi-dry sausage, preserved meat or preserved meat by-product, it must be packaged separately from any spice or seasoning.

rows.foods: (d) Mold ripened cheese packaged in hermetically sealed containers
rows.max: (d) If used singly, the amount not to exceed 200 ppm of the milk and milk products used to manufacture the cheese. If used in combination with potassium nitrate, the total combined amount not to exceed 200 ppm of the milk and milk products used to manufacture the cheese. In either case, the amount not to exceed 50 ppm in the finished cheese.

rows.foods: (e) Ripened cheese, containing not more than 68% moisture on a fat free basis during manufacture of which the lactic acid fermentation and salting is completed later than 12 hours after coagulation of the curd by food enzymes and where the added salt is applied externally to the cheese as dry salt or in the form of brine
rows.max: (e) If used singly, the amount not to exceed 200 ppm of the milk and milk products used to manufacture the cheese. If used in combination with potassium nitrate, the total combined amount not to exceed 200 ppm of the milk and milk products used to manufacture the cheese. In either case, the amount not to exceed 50 ppm in the finished cheese.

overview: Sodium nitrate (E 251) is a food additive. The official lists name this function: preservative.
The EU specification describes it as: “White crystalline, slightly hygroscopic powder.”
In the EU it may be used in 9 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; meat; fish and fisheries products.
In the US it is listed as Sodium Nitrate: approved food additive (21 CFR 172).
Canada permits it (on the List of Permitted Preservatives).
Australia and New Zealand permit it in specific foods (Schedule 15 of the Food Standards Code).

overview: Potassium nitrate (E 252) is a food additive. The official lists name this function: preservative.
The EU specification describes it as: “White crystalline powder or transparent prisms having a cooling, saline, pungent taste.”
In the EU it may be used in 9 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; meat; fish and fisheries products.
In the US it is listed as Potassium Nitrate: approved food additive (21 CFR 172).
Canada permits it (on the List of Permitted Preservatives).
Australia and New Zealand permit it in specific foods (Schedule 15 of the Food Standards Code).

overview: Sodium ascorbate (E 301) is a food additive. The official lists name this function: preservative.
The EU specification describes it as: “White or almost white, odourless crystalline powder which darkens on exposure to light.”
In the EU it may be used in 77 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; fats and oils and fat and oil emulsions; edible ices; fruit and vegetables…
In the US it is listed as Sodium Ascorbate: listed as GRAS (21 CFR 182).
Canada permits it (on the List of Permitted Preservatives).
Australia and New Zealand permit it as a food additive.

identity.definition: Oat lecithin is a fractionated oat oil rich in polar lipids, mainly galactolipids. Oat lecithin is produced from food grade oat kernels that are sieved and extracted using ethanol at an elevated temperature to produce a crude lipid extract. This crude extract undergoes multistage evaporation and filtration, yielding crude oat oil, which is separated, evaporated and filtered to produce oat lecithin. Only ethanol may be used in the extraction as extraction solvent.

overview: Citric acid (E 330) is a food additive. The official lists name these functions: acidity regulator and preservative.
The EU specification describes it as: “Citric acid is a white or colourless, odourless, crystalline solid, having a strongly acid taste.”
In the EU it may be used in 84 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; fats and oils and fat and oil emulsions; edible ices; fruit and vegetables…
In the US it is listed as Citric Acid: affirmed as GRAS (21 CFR 184).
Canada permits it (on 4 of Health Canada's permitted lists).
Australia and New Zealand permit it as a food additive.

overview: Potassium citrates (E 332) is a food additive. The official lists name these functions: emulsifier and acidity regulator.
The EU specification describes it as: “White, hygroscopic, granular powder or transparent crystals.”
In the EU it may be used in 77 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; fats and oils and fat and oil emulsions; edible ices; fruit and vegetables…
In the US it is listed as Potassium Citrate: affirmed as GRAS (21 CFR 184).
Canada permits it as Potassium Citrate (on 2 of Health Canada's permitted lists).
Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Potassium citrate; Potassium dihydrogen citrate) as a food additive.

overview: Sodium potassium tartrate (E 337) is a food additive. The official lists name these functions: emulsifier and acidity regulator.
The EU specification describes it as: “Colourless crystals or white crystalline powder.”
In the EU it may be used in 30 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; fats and oils and fat and oil emulsions; fruit and vegetables; confectionery…
In the US it is listed as Sodium Potassium Tartrate: affirmed as GRAS (21 CFR 184).
Canada permits it (on 2 of Health Canada's permitted lists).
Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Potassium sodium tartrate) as a food additive.

overview: Sodium phosphates (E 339) is a food additive. The official lists name these functions: stabiliser, emulsifier and colour.
The EU specification describes it as: “A white odourless, slightly deliquescent powder, crystals or granules.”
In the EU it may be used in 60 food categories, in these food groups: all foods; dairy products and analogues; fats and oils and fat and oil emulsions; edible ices…
In the US it is listed as Sodium Phosphate, Dibasic: listed as GRAS (21 CFR 182).
Canada permits it as Sodium Phosphate, Dibasic; Sodium Phosphate, Monobasic; Sodium Phosphate, Tribasic (on 4 of Health Canada's permitted lists).
Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Sodium phosphate, dibasic; Sodium phosphate, monobasic) as a food additive.

overview: Potassium phosphates (E 340) is a food additive. The official lists name these functions: stabiliser, emulsifier and colour.
The EU specification describes it as: “Odourless, colourless crystals or white granular or crystalline powder.”
In the EU it may be used in 60 food categories, in these food groups: all foods; dairy products and analogues; fats and oils and fat and oil emulsions; edible ices…
In the US it is listed as Dipotassium Phosphate: listed as GRAS (21 CFR 182).
Canada permits it as Potassium Phosphate, Dibasic; Potassium Phosphate, Monobasic; Potassium Phosphate, Tribasic (on 5 of Health Canada's permitted lists).
Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Potassium phosphate, dibasic; Potassium phosphate, monobasic) as a food additive.

overview: Calcium phosphates (E 341) is a food additive. The official lists name these functions: anti-caking agent, emulsifier and carrier or solvent.
The EU specification describes it as: “Granular powder or white, deliquescent crystals or granules.”
In the EU it may be used in 60 food categories, in these food groups: all foods; dairy products and analogues; fats and oils and fat and oil emulsions; edible ices…
In the US it is listed as Calcium Phosphate, Tribasic: listed as GRAS (21 CFR 182).
Canada permits it as Calcium Phosphate, Dibasic; Calcium Phosphate, Monobasic; Calcium Phosphate, Tribasic (on 7 of Health Canada's permitted lists).
Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Calcium phosphate, dibasic or calcium hydrogen phosphate; Calcium phosphate, monobasic or calcium dihydrogen phosphate) as a food additive.

In the EU it may be used in 57 food categories, in these food groups: all foods; dairy products and analogues; fats and oils and fat and oil emulsions; edible ices…
In the US it is listed as Magnesium Phosphate, Tribasic: affirmed as GRAS (21 CFR 184).
Canada permits it as Magnesium Phosphate (on the List of Permitted Acidity Regulators and Acid-Reacting Materials).
Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Magnesium phosphate, dibasic; Magnesium phosphate, monobasic) as a food additive.

The EU specification describes it as: “White, odourless crystalline granules or white to nearly white powder, slightly hygroscopic.”
In the EU it may be used in 6 food categories, in these food groups: fats and oils and fat and oil emulsions; fruit and vegetables; meat; fish and fisheries products…
In the US it is listed as EDTA, Calcium Disodium: colour additive for food, exempt from certification (21 CFR 73.1).
Canada permits it as Calcium Disodium Ethylenediaminetetraacetate (Calcium Disodium EDTA) (on the List of Permitted Sequestering Agents).
Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Calcium disodium ethylenediaminetetraacetate or calcium disodium EDTA) in specific foods (Schedule 15 of the Food Standards Code).

To a 0,5 % solution of the sample in 1 M sodium hydroxide solution add one fifth of its volume of a 2,5 % solution of calcium chloride. A voluminous, gelatinous precipitate is formed. overview: Alginic acid (E 400) is a food additive. The official lists name these functions: emulsifier and thickener.
The EU specification describes it as: “Alginic acid occurs in filamentous, grainy, granular and powdered forms.”
In the EU it may be used in 67 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; fats and oils and fat and oil emulsions; edible ices; fruit and vegetables…
In the US it is listed as Alginic Acid: affirmed as GRAS (21 CFR 184).
Canada permits it (on the List of Permitted Emulsifying, Gelling, Stabilizing or Thickening Agents).
Australia and New Zealand permit it as a food additive.

identity.definition: Carrageenan is obtained by extraction with water or dilute aqueous alkali of strains of seaweeds of Gigartinaceae, Solieriaceae, Hypneaceae and Furcellariaceae, families of the class Rhodophyceae (red seaweeds). Carrageenan consists chiefly of the potassium, sodium, magnesium and calcium sulphate esters of galactose and 3,6-anhydrogalactose polysacharide. These hexoses are alternately linked α-1,3 and β-1,4 in the copolymer. The prevalent polysaccharides in carrageenan are designated as kappa, iota, lambda depending on the number of sulphate by repeating unit (i.e. 1,2,3 sulphate). Between kappa and iota there is a continuum of intermediate compositions differing in number of sulphates per repeat units between 1 and 2. During the process, no organic precipitant shall be used other than methanol, ethanol and propan-2-ol. The wording carrageenan is reserved for the non hydrolysed or otherwise chemically degraded polymer. Formaldehyde may be present as an adventitious impurity up to a maximum of 5 mg/kg.

overview: Carrageenan (E 407) is a food additive. The official lists name these functions: gelling agent, thickener and emulsifier.
The EU specification describes it as: “Yellowish to colourless, coarse to fine powder which is practically odourless.”
In the EU it may be used in 73 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; fats and oils and fat and oil emulsions; edible ices; fruit and vegetables…
In the US it is listed as Furcelleran and Salts of Furcelleran: approved food additive (21 CFR 172).
Canada permits it as Ammonium Carrageenan; Ammonium Furcelleran; Calcium Carrageenan; Calcium Furcelleran (on the List of Permitted Emulsifying, Gelling, Stabilizing or Thickening Agents).
Australia and New Zealand permit it as a food additive.

identity.definition: Processed eucheuma seaweed is obtained by aqueous alkaline (KOH) treatment at high temperature of the strains of seaweeds Eucheuma cottonii and Eucheuma spinosum, of the class Rhodophyceae (red seaweeds) followed by fresh water washing to remove impurities and drying to obtain the product. Further purification may be achieved by washing with an alcohol. The alcohols authorised are restricted to methanol, ethanol or propan-2-ol. The product consists chiefly of the potassium, sodium, magnesium and calcium sulphate esters of galactose and 3,6-anhydrogalactose polysaccharide. Up to 15 % algal cellulose is also present in the product. The wording processed eucheuma seaweed is reserved to the non hydrolysed or otherwise chemically degraded polymer. Formaldehyde may be present up to a maximum of 5 mg/kg.

identity.definition: Locust bean gum is the ground endosperm of the seeds of the strainsof carob tree, Cerationia siliqua (L.) Taub. (family Leguminosae). The seeds are dehusked by treating the kernels with dilute sulfuric acid or with thermal mechanical treatments, elimination of the germ, followed by milling and screening of the endosperm to obtain native locust bean gum. Locust bean gum consists mainly of a high molecular weight hydrocolloidal polysaccharide, composed of galactopyranose and mannopyranose units combined through glycosidic linkages, which may be described chemically as galactomannan.
identity.description: White to yellowish-white, nearly odourless powder
identity.assay: Galactomannan content not less than 75 %
identity.solubility: Fully dispersible in hot water, insoluble in ethanol
identification: Place some ground sample in an aqueous solution containing 0,5 % iodine and 1 % potassium iodide on a glass slide and examine under microscope. Locust bean gum contains long stretched tubiform cells, separated or slightly interspaced. Their brown contents are much less regularly formed than in guar
Fully dispersible in hot water, insoluble in ethanol

identity.definition: Tragacanth is a dried exudation obtained from the stems and branches of strains of Astragalus gummifer Labillardiere and other Asiatic species of Astragalus (family Leguminosae). It consists mainly of high molecular weight polysaccharides (galactoarabans and acidic polysaccharides) which, on hydrolysis, yield galacturonic acid, galactose, arabinose, xylose and fucose. Small amounts of rhamnose and of glucose (derived from traces of starch and/or cellulose) may also be present
identity.description: Unground Tragacanth gum occurs as flattened, lamellated, straight or curved fragments or as spirally twisted pieces 0,5-2,5 mm thick and up to 3 cm in length. It is white to pale yellow in colour but some pieces may have a red tinge. The pieces are horny in texture, with a short fracture. It is odourless and solutions have an insipid mucilaginous taste. Powdered tragacanth is white to pale yellow or pinkish brown (pale tan) in colour
identity.solubility: 1 g of the sample in 50 ml of water swells to form a smooth, stiff, opalescent mucilage; insoluble in ethanol and does not swell in 60 % (w/v) aqueous ethanol
identification: 1 g of the sample in 50 ml of water swells to form a smooth, stiff, opalescent mucilage; insoluble in ethanol and does not swell in 60 % (w/v) aqueous ethanol
purity: Negative. Boil 1 g with 20 ml of water until a mucilage is formed. Add 5 ml of hydrochloric acid and again boil the mixture for five minutes. No permanent pink or red colour develops

identity.definition: Acacia gum is a dried exudation obtained from the stems and branches of strains of Acacia senegal (L) Willdenow or closely related species of Acacia (family Leguminosae). It consists mainly of high molecular weight polysaccharides and their calcium, magnesium and potassium salts, which on hydrolysis yield arabinose, galactose, rhamnose and glucuronic acid.
identity.description: Unground acacia gum occurs as white or yellowish-white spheroidal tears of varying sizes or as angular fragments and is sometimes mixed with darker fragments. It is also available in the form of white to yellowish-white flakes, granules, powder or spray-dried material.
identity.solubility: 1 g dissolves in 2 ml of cold water forming a dispersion which flows readily and is acid to litmus, insoluble in ethanol.

overview: Gum arabic (acacia gum) (E 414) is a food additive. The official lists name these functions: emulsifier, thickener and glazing agent.
The EU specification describes it as: “Unground acacia gum occurs as white or yellowish-white spheroidal tears of varying sizes or as angular fragments and is sometimes mixed with darker fragments.”
In the EU it may be used in 69 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; fats and oils and fat and oil emulsions; edible ices; fruit and vegetables…
In the US it is listed as Acacia, Gum (Acacia Senegal (L.) Willd.): affirmed as GRAS (21 CFR 184).
Canada permits it as Acacia Gum (on 3 of Health Canada's permitted lists).
Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Acacia or gum arabic) as a food additive.

identity.definition: Xanthan gum is a high molecular weight polysaccharide gum produced by a pure-culture fermentation of a carbohydrate with strains of Xanthomonas campestris, which are unequivocally identified and meet the criteria for qualification for QPS status (i.e. absence of acquired antimicrobial resistance genes), purified by recovery with ethanol or propan-2-ol, dried and milled. identity.definition: Konjac gum is a water-soluble hydrocolloid obtained from the Konjac flour by aqueous extraction. Konjac flour is the unpurified raw product from the root of the perennial plant Amorphophallus konjac. The main component of Konjac gum is the water-soluble high-molecular-weight polysaccharide glucomannan, which consists of D-mannose and D-glucose units at a molar ratio of 1,6:1,0, connected by β(1-4)-glycosidic bonds. Shorter side chains are attached through β(1-3)-glycosidic bonds, and acetyl groups occur at random at a ratio of about 1 group per 9 to 19 sugar units

identity.definition: A complex mixture of tri- and diglycerol esters of resin acids from wood rosin. The rosin is obtained by the solvent extraction of aged pine stumps followed by a liquid-liquid solvent refining process. Excluded from these specifications are substances derived from gum rosin, and exudate of living pine trees, and substances derived from tall oil rosin, a by-product of kraft (paper) pulp processing. The final product is composed of approximately 90 % resin acids and 10 % neutrals (non-acidic compounds). The resin acid fraction is a complex mixture of isomeric diterpenoid monocarboxylic acids having the empirical molecular formula of C20H30O2, chiefly abietic acid. The substance is purified by steam stripping or by countercurrent steam distillation

overview: Triphosphates (E 451) is a food additive. The official lists name these functions: stabiliser and acidity regulator.
The EU specification describes it as: “White, slightly hygroscopic granules or powder.”
In the EU it may be used in 57 food categories, in these food groups: all foods; dairy products and analogues; fats and oils and fat and oil emulsions; edible ices…
In the US it is listed as Potassium Tripolyphosphate: approved secondary direct food additive (21 CFR 173).
Canada permits it as Potassium Tripolyphosphate; Sodium Potassium Tripolyphosphate; Sodium Tripolyphosphate (on 5 of Health Canada's permitted lists).
Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Potassium tripolyphosphate; Sodium tripolyphosphate) as a food additive.

identity.definition: Soluble sodium polyphosphates are obtained by fusion and subsequent chilling of sodium orthophosphates. These compounds are a class consisting of several amorphous, water-soluble polyphosphates composed of linear chains of metaphosphate units, (NaPO3)x where x ≥ 2, terminated by Na2PO4 groups. These substances are usually identified by their Na2O/P2O5 ratio or their P2O5 content. The Na2O/P2O5 ratios vary from about 1,3 for sodium tetrapolyphosphate, where x = approximately 4; to about 1,1 for Graham's salt, commonly called sodium hexametaphosphate, where x = 13 to 18; and to about 1,0 for the higher molecular weight sodium polyphosphates, where x = 20 to 100 or more. The pH of their solutions varies from 3,0 to 9,0

overview: Polyphosphates (E 452) is a food additive. The official lists name these functions: stabiliser, emulsifier and acidity regulator.
The EU specification describes it as: “Colourless or white, transparent platelets, granules, or powders.”
In the EU it may be used in 57 food categories, in these food groups: all foods; dairy products and analogues; fats and oils and fat and oil emulsions; edible ices…
In the US it is listed as Sodium Hexametaphosphate: listed as GRAS (21 CFR 182).
Canada permits it as Sodium Hexametaphosphate; Sodium Potassium Hexametaphosphate (on 4 of Health Canada's permitted lists).
Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Potassium polymetaphosphate; Sodium metaphosphate, insoluble) as a food additive.

identity.definition: Potassium polyaspartate is the potassium salt of polyaspartic acid, produced from L-aspartic acid and potassium hydroxide. The thermic process transforms the aspartic acid in polysuccinimide that is insoluble. Polysuccinimide is treated with potassium hydroxide allowing the opening of the ring and polymerisation of the units. The last step is the spray drying phase, which results in a light tan powder

identity.definition: L-HPC is a low-substituted poly (hydroxypropyl) ether of cellulose. L-HPC is manufactured by partial etherification of the anhydroglucose units of pure cellulose (wood pulp) with propylene oxide/hydroxypropyl groups. The resulting product is then purified, dried and milled to yield low-substituted hydroxypropyl cellulose. L-HPC contains not less than 5,0 % and not more than 16,0 % of hydroxypropoxy groups, calculated on the dried basis. L-HPC differs from hydroxypropyl cellulose (E 463) with respect to the degree of molar substitution with hydroxypropoxy groups of the glucose ring unit (0,2 for L-HPC vs 3,5 for E 463) of the cellulose backbone.

identity.solubility: Insoluble in water; swelling in water. It dissolves in a solution of 10 % sodium hydroxide producing a viscous solution.
purity: Not more than 0,1 mg/kg (on an anhydrous basis) (gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS))

overview: Magnesium salts of fatty acids (E 470b) is a food additive. The official lists name this function: anti-caking agent.
The EU specification describes it as: “White or creamy-white light powders, flakes or semi-solids.”
In the EU it may be used in 65 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; fats and oils and fat and oil emulsions; edible ices; fruit and vegetables…
In the US it is listed as Magnesium Salts of Fatty Acids: approved food additive (21 CFR 172).
Canada permits it as Magnesium Stearate (on 2 of Health Canada's permitted lists).
Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Fatty acid salts of aluminium, ammonia, calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium) as a food additive.

overview: Mono-and diglycerides of fatty acids (E 471) is a food additive. The official lists name these functions: emulsifier, anti-foaming agent and humectant.
The EU specification describes it as: “The product varies from a pale yellow to pale brown oily liquid to a white or slightly off-white hard waxy solid.”
In the EU it may be used in 79 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; fats and oils and fat and oil emulsions; edible ices; fruit and vegetables…
In the US it is listed as Glyceryl Monooleate: affirmed as GRAS (21 CFR 184).
Canada permits it as Mono- and Diglycerides; Monoglycerides (on 3 of Health Canada's permitted lists).
Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Mono- and di-glycerides of fatty acids) as a food additive.

overview: Citric acid esters of mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids (E 472c) is a food additive. The official lists name these functions: emulsifier and preservative.
The EU specification describes it as: “Yellowish or light brown liquids to waxy solids or semi-solids.”
In the EU it may be used in 69 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; fats and oils and fat and oil emulsions; edible ices; fruit and vegetables…
In the US it is listed as Monoglyceride Citrate: approved food additive (21 CFR 172).
Canada permits it as Citric Acid Esters of Mono- and Diglycerides; Monoglyceride Citrate (on 3 of Health Canada's permitted lists).
Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Citric and fatty acid esters of glycerol) as a food additive.

In the EU it may be used in 64 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; fats and oils and fat and oil emulsions; edible ices; fruit and vegetables…
In the US it is listed as Potassium Chloride: affirmed as GRAS (21 CFR 184).
Canada permits it (on 3 of Health Canada's permitted lists).
Australia and New Zealand permit it as a food additive.

overview: Sodium gluconate (E 576) is a food additive. The official lists name these functions: emulsifier and acidity regulator.
The EU specification describes it as: “White to tan, granular to fine, crystalline powder.”
In the EU it may be used in 66 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; fats and oils and fat and oil emulsions; edible ices; fruit and vegetables…
In the US it is listed as Sodium Gluconate: listed as GRAS (21 CFR 182).
Canada permits it (on 2 of Health Canada's permitted lists).
Australia and New Zealand permit it as a food additive.

Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Disodium-5′-guanylate) as a food additive.

overview: Nitrous oxide (E 942) is a food additive. FDA's inventory lists these technical effects: flavour enhancer and propellant.
The EU specification describes it as: “Colourless, non-flammable gas, sweetish odour.”
In the EU it may be used in 65 food categories, in these food groups: all foods; dairy products and analogues; fats and oils and fat and oil emulsions; edible ices…
In the US it is listed as Nitrous Oxide: affirmed as GRAS (21 CFR 184).
Canada permits it (on the List of Permitted Food Additives with Other Purposes of Use).
Australia and New Zealand permit it as a food additive.

overview: Saccharins (E 954) is a food additive. The official lists name this function: sweetener.
The EU specification describes it as: “White crystals or a white crystalline powder, odourless or with a faint, aromatic odour.”
In the EU it may be used in 34 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; edible ices; fruit and vegetables; confectionery…
In the US it is listed as Saccharin, Calcium Salt: interim food additive (21 CFR 180).
Canada permits it as Calcium Saccharin; Potassium Saccharin; Saccharin; Sodium Saccharin (on the List of Permitted Sweeteners).
Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Saccharin) in specific foods (Schedule 15 of the Food Standards Code).

The additive may contain residues of ion-exchange resins used in the manufacturing process. identity.definition: Rebaudioside M is a steviol glycoside composed predominantly of rebaudioside M with minor amounts of other steviol glycosides such as rebaudioside A, rebaudioside B, rebaudioside D, rebaudioside I, and stevioside. Rebaudioside M is obtained via enzymatic bioconversion of puriﬁed steviol glycoside leaf extracts (95% steviol glycosides) of the Stevia rebaudiana Bertoni plant using UDP-glucosyltransferase and sucrose synthase enzymes produced by the genetically modified yeasts K. phaffi (formerly known as Pichia pastoris) UGT-a and K. phaffi UGT-b that facilitate the transfer of glucose from sucrose and UDP-glucose to steviol glycosides via glycosidic bonds. After removal of the enzymes by solid-liquid separation and heat treatment, the purification involves concentration of the rebaudioside M by resin adsorption, followed by recrystallisation of rebaudioside M resulting in a final product containing not less than 95 % of rebaudioside M. Viable cells of the yeasts K. phafﬁi UGT-a and K. phafﬁi UGT-b and their DNA shall not be detected in the food additive. ◄
identity.description: White to light yellow powder, approximately between 200 and 350 times sweeter than sucrose (at 5 % sucrose equivalency).
identity.spec_title: Rebaudioside m produced via enzyme modification of steviol glycosides from stevia
identity.assay: Not less than 95 % rebaudioside M on the dried basis.
identity.solubility: Freely soluble to slightly soluble in water
identification: Freely soluble to slightly soluble in water
purity: Not less than 74 μm [using a mesh #200 sieve with a particle size limit of 74 μm]

identity.definition: Mixture of larger glycosides of steviol derived by glucosylation of steviol glycosides extracted from leaves of Stevia rebaudiana Bertoni plant. The mixture is composed of glucosylated steviol glycosides and residual parent steviol glycosides from Stevia leaf. Glucosylated steviol glycosides are produced by treating the steviol glycosides, extracted from Stevia leaf, and starch suitable for human consumption with Cyclomaltodextrin glucanotransferase (EC 2.4.1.19) derived from a non-GMO strain of Anoxybacillus caldiproteolyticus St-88. The enzyme transfers glucose units from the starch to the steviol glycosides. The resulting material is heated and treated with activated carbon to remove the enzyme, then passed through adsorption/desorption resin to remove residual hydrolysed starch (dextrin), followed by purification and preparation of the final product using processes that may include decolourisation, concentration and spray drying.
identity.description: White to light yellow powder, approximately between 100 and 200 times sweeter than sucrose (at 5 % sucrose equivalency).
identity.assay: Not less than 95 % of total steviol glycosides, comprised of above mentioned steviol glycosides along with their glucosylated derivatives (1-20 added glucose units), on the dried, dextrin-free, basis.
identity.solubility: Soluble in water
purity: Not more than 200 mg/kg methanol Not more than 3 000 mg/kg ethanol

overview: Glucosylated steviol glycosides (E 960d) is a food additive. The official lists name this function: sweetener.
The EU specification describes it as: “White to light yellow powder, approximately between 100 and 200 times sweeter than sucrose (at 5 % sucrose equivalency).”
In the EU it may be used in 32 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; edible ices; fruit and vegetables; confectionery…
In Great Britain: not in the GB register of authorised food additives.
EU history: added to the EU list, first shown in the consolidated text of 22 March 2023.
Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Steviol glycosides) in specific foods (Schedule 15 of the Food Standards Code).

identity.definition: Neotame is manufactured by reaction under hydrogen pressure of aspartame with 3,3,-dimethylbutyraldehyde in methanol in presence of a palladium/carbon catalyst. It is isolated and purified by filtration, where diatomaceous earth may be used. After solvent removal via distillation, neotame is washed with water, isolated by centrifugation and finally vacuum dried.

overview: Salt of aspartame-acesulfame (E 962) is a food additive. The official lists name this function: sweetener.
The EU specification describes it as: “A white, odourless, crystalline powder.”
In the EU it may be used in 34 food categories, in these food groups: dairy products and analogues; edible ices; fruit and vegetables; confectionery…
Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Aspartame-acesulphame salt) in specific foods (Schedule 15 of the Food Standards Code).

identity.definition: A mixture consisting mainly of maltitol and sorbitol and lesser amounts of hydrogenated oligo- and polysaccharides and maltrotriitol. It is manufactured by the catalytic hydrogenation of a mixture of starch hydrolysates consisting of glucose, maltose and higher glucose polymers, similar to the catalytic hydrogenation process used for the manufacture of maltitol syrup. The resulting syrup is desalted by ion exchange and concentrated to the desired level.
identity.description: Colourless and odourless clear viscous liquid
synonyms: Hydrogenated starch hydrolysate, hydrogenated glucose syrup and polyglucitol
identity.assay: Content not less than 99 % of total hydrogenated saccharides on the anhydrous basis, not less than 50 % higher molecular weight polyols, not more than 50 % of maltitol and not more than 20 % of sorbitol on the anhydrous basis.
identity.solubility: Very soluble in water and slightly soluble in ethanol

identity.definition: Advantame (ANS9801) is produced by chemical synthesis in a three-step process; production of the principal manufacturing intermediate, 3-hydroxy-4-methoxycinnamaldehyde (HMCA), followed by hydrogenation to form 3-(3-hydroxy-4-methoxyphenyl) propionaldehyde (HMPA). overview: Polyethylene glycol (E 1521) is a food additive. The official lists name this function: anti-foaming agent.

Australia and New Zealand permit it (listed as Polyethylene glycol 8000) as a food additive.
